sections.markdown:
## C — Driving conditions part two: towing and trailer limits, recreational vehicle combinations, winter driving, snowplows and winter survival, staying alert, skids and anti-lock brakes, rain, fog and hydroplaning, blowouts and steering, brake and other vehicle failures, deer, oncoming and passing threats, rail stalls, floods, submersion, fire, overheating, power lines and carbon monoxide
Knowledge domain: how to tow safely within Minnesota's trailer limits, drive and survive in winter, stay alert, recover from skids and hydroplaning, and respond to vehicle failures, roadway threats, floods, fires, downed power lines and carbon monoxide.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
When towing, speed up carefully in a lower gear if needed, keep enough following distance to avoid sudden stops, and remember the trailer's extra length and your slower acceleration when passing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
A trailer may be at most 45 feet long, 8 feet 6 inches wide and 13 feet 6 inches high. [A01]
Why it matters: the trailer size limits are likely numeric items.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
A trailer needs two red tail lamps, two red reflectors and one white rear license plate lamp, and its own stop and turn signals at night or whenever the towing vehicle's signals cannot be seen. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
A trailer may not be wider than the towing vehicle's exterior rearview mirrors. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
Every trailer with a gross vehicle weight of 3,000 pounds or more must have brakes. [A01]
Why it matters: the trailer brake weight is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
You must be at least 18 to drive a recreational vehicle combination, and the pickup or truck-tractor's towing rating must at least equal the total weight being towed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
A recreational vehicle combination may be no longer than 70 feet and may not be driven in the Twin Cities Metro Area on weekdays from 6 to 9 a.m. or 4 to 7 p.m. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A02
Before driving in winter, clear snow and ice from the hood, windows and lights, and use windshield washer fluid that contains antifreeze. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A02
Get the feel of a winter road by testing your brakes at low speed, adjust your speed to conditions, and avoid cruise control on slippery roads. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
To rock a vehicle out of snow or ice, keep the front wheels straight, ease forward and then backward as far as you can without spinning the tires, and accelerate gently once they grip. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Snowplows show flashing white, yellow and blue lights; never crowd one, pass only when you can see the whole plow, and stay well back from the sand, snow and ice it throws. [A02]
Why it matters: snowplow passing is a Minnesota-specific item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
A winter survival kit should include items such as a shovel, sand or salt, warm clothing, a red flag for the antenna, a blanket, quick energy food and water, chains, flares, jumper cables, candles and matches, and a first aid kit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A03
If you are stranded in cold weather, stay with your vehicle, because most deaths happen when people leave, get lost and suffer long exposure to the cold. [A03]
Why it matters: staying with the vehicle is a classic winter survival item.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A03
While stranded, run the engine and heater for about 10 minutes each hour, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow, and leave at least one window partly open to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A03
On a long drive, stop at least every 100 miles or every two hours to walk, stretch and have something to eat or drink. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A03
If you skid, stay calm and do not overreact or slam on the brakes; slow down and keep a safe gap on slippery roads to avoid skids in the first place. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A04
With anti-lock brakes, do not pump the pedal; press down firmly and keep steering until you regain control. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A04
In thunderstorms or fog, slow down, increase your following distance, keep headlights on low beam to cut glare, and pull off the road if you cannot see a safe distance ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A04
Hydroplaning happens when water collects under the tires at higher speeds and lifts them off the road, and in heavy rain standard cars may start to hydroplane at 35 mph. [A04]
Why it matters: the hydroplaning speed is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A04
If your tires hydroplane you cannot brake, accelerate or steer, so take your foot off the gas pedal. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A04
Hydroplaning can happen at any speed when the water on the road is deeper than the tire tread, so keep tires in good condition and slow down on wet roads. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A04
In a blowout, grip the wheel firmly, steer straight, ease off the accelerator, do not brake until the vehicle is under control, and then pull completely off the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A05
If the steering stops responding, ease off the accelerator and brake only if needed to avoid a crash, and then gently, since sudden braking or shifting can throw the vehicle out of control. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A05
If the brake pedal drops to the floor, pump it to build pressure, and if that fails, apply the emergency or parking brake slowly, remembering it works only on the rear wheels. [A05]
Why it matters: the parking brake works on the rear wheels only.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A05
If your wheels drift onto the shoulder, do not swerve back; stay on the shoulder, ease off the gas, and turn back onto the pavement only after slowing down. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A05
Deer are most active from dusk to dawn, so watch for eye reflections along the roadside, slow down, sound the horn, be ready to stop and expect more than one deer. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A05
If a vehicle comes toward you in your lane, move right rather than left, and steer off the road to the right if needed, using the horn and headlights to alert the driver. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A05
If a passing driver on a two-lane road is nearly back in the right lane, slow down to let them finish, but if they must drop back, speed up to leave room behind you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A06
If your vehicle stalls on tracks with a train coming, get out immediately and walk quickly away at a 45-degree angle in the direction the train is coming from. [A06]
Why it matters: the escape direction is a frequently missed item.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A06
Never drive through a flooded road; turn around and find another route, or wait on higher ground if there is none. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A06
Six inches of water reaches the underside of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling, and 2 feet of moving water is enough to sweep away most vehicles, SUVs and pickups included. [A06]
Why it matters: the flood depths are likely numeric items.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A06
Most vehicles float for 30 to 60 seconds after entering deep water, so get out right away, through open windows if possible, before the water reaches them. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A06
If you see smoke rising from under the hood, pull off the road, turn off the ignition and get out at once, and never use water on the fire because it spreads the blaze. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A06
If the engine overheats, turn off extras such as the air conditioning, then turn on the heater to draw heat away, and if the temperature still climbs or steam appears, pull over and shut off the ignition. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A07
If the gas pedal sticks, try lifting it with your toe, and if that fails, brake, shift into neutral and steer to the shoulder. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A07
If your vehicle hits a utility pole, wire or power box, stay inside and call 911, and get out only if it is on fire. [A07]
Why it matters: staying inside is the key power line rule.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A07
If you must leave a vehicle touching power equipment, jump clear with both feet together and shuffle away, assuming every wire is electrified. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec12-F38 | anchor: A07
Carbon monoxide is a deadly, odorless, colorless engine gas, and the only cure for poisoning is plenty of fresh air. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec12-F39 | anchor: A07
Early signs of carbon monoxide poisoning are sudden fatigue, headache, dizziness and nausea, and if they appear, open the windows, turn off the ignition and get out. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec12-F40 | anchor: A08
Carbon monoxide poisoning is most common in winter, can build up in a garage even with the door fully open, and can knock a person unconscious within a few minutes. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec12-F41 | anchor: A08
To lower carbon monoxide risk, warm up the vehicle in the driveway rather than the garage, avoid sitting in an idling vehicle, and do not idle when stuck in snow or mud. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0090]

Misconceptions: anti-lock brakes are not pumped; a hydroplaning car cannot be steered or braked, so lift off the gas; when stranded in winter you stay with the vehicle; after touching a power line you stay inside unless there is a fire; water does not put out an engine fire; shallow-looking floodwater is still unsafe.
Mnemonics: forty-five long, eight and a half wide, thirteen and a half high; brakes from three thousand pounds; ten minutes an hour, window cracked; walk toward the train at an angle; six inches costs you control, two feet carries the car away.
Glossary: anti-lock braking system means an electronic system that helps keep the vehicle under control while braking; hydroplaning means tires riding on a film of water and losing contact with the road; blowout means a sudden tire burst; whiteout means blowing snow that hides the road; recreational vehicle combination means a pickup or truck-tractor towing a camper trailer that may tow another trailer; carbon monoxide means an odorless, colorless gas from engines.
Dynamic facts: the Twin Cities Metro Area weekday rush-hour ban on recreational vehicle combinations is tied to a place and times of day; recheck it against an official DPS or DVS source before each release.
